h.strategy: Obvious hypotheses (an edit matters more when an alternative path is removed; strong components help more when connected) score zero even if true. Target effects that real measurements often show but intuition misses: ceiling effects (a normally helpful edit helps less, or hurts, when the parent is already strong); redundancy (two strong components in parallel are worth less than either alone suggests); substitution (a cheap or 'weak' option beats a strong one when capacity elsewhere is high); and sign reversals of an edit's usual effect under specific conditions. Each hypothesis needs a concrete mechanism. Vary the edited field and the conditioning field across hypotheses, and include both HIGHER and LOWER directions.

hyps.why: With a skip shortcut already carrying the signal to the output, a stronger edge 0 helps less (ceiling).
Removing the direct edge costs less when a strong conv path into node 3 exists, because it is redundant.
With a 3x3 already feeding node 2, a cheap 1x1 on edge 2 matches the larger conv at lower cost, so the substitution works.
Pooling after a strong conv at node 1 acts as a useful smoother and loses little relative to the alternatives.
With a conv already on the chain feeding node 2, a skip on edge 5 preserves depth while keeping gradients clean.
Two 1x1 convs in parallel into the output add redundant low-capacity paths.
Pooling on edge 0 loses less when the other input branch already supplies a strong conv path.
A skip on edge 1 complements a conv branch on edge 0 and gives a mixed shallow and deep representation.
Two parallel skips into the output are redundant and add no extra representation.
A cheap pool on edge 2 costs little when a strong conv on edge 4 already provides node 1's contribution to the output.
